Science Programs The DOE Office of Science sponsors basic research at over 300 institutions across the country, including universities, national laboratories, nonprofits, and private sector institutions. Funding is awarded on a competitive basis using peer review. Research efforts range from single-investigator grants to large team-based projects. We administer research through eight program offices, spanning a broad range of disciplines: Accelerator R&D and Production , Advanced Scientific Computing Research , Basic Energy Sciences , Biological and Environmental Research , Fusion Energy Sciences , High Energy and Nuclear Physics , and Isotope R&D and Production . The DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program provides annual funding opportunities for outstanding early career scientists in the disciplines supported by the DOE Office of Science. In addition, our Office of Workforce Development for Teachers and Scientists sponsors student internships and other education and training programs at DOE’s 17 national laboratories. Image courtesy of Alex Parsons, Facility for Rare Isotope Beams, Michigan State University. The Science Nuclear beta decay occurs when atomic nuclei with too many neutrons or protons emit particles. The nuclei either converts a proton to a neutron or vice versa. In “forbidden beta decays,” a nucleus decays into another nucleus, an electron, and a neutrino. However, in the process, it violates certain “selection rules” imposed by parity and rotational symmetry, both fundamental physics concepts. Scientists thought one of these types of forbidden beta decays was completely blocked in certain circumstances. However, this study reveals that these modes of nuclear decay can occur due to quantum corrections. Now a new and far smaller tyrannosaur is filling in the famous dinosaur’s evolutionary backstory. pages.text: Scientists find a new titanosaur dinosaur species in Patagonia | National Geographic Premium SCIENCE Scientists find a new titanosaur dinosaur species in Patagonia The new Argentine dino might give us clues to what the world was like before the asteroid wiped out their kind. Hundreds of fossils found at a quarry in Northern Patagonia provide a snapshot of what a desert pond ecosystem might have looked like in the late Cretaceous period. Researchers found a previously undiscovered species of titanosaur (illustrated above) among other fossilized creatures at the site. Illustration by Gabriel Lio By Meghie Rodrigues Published March 5, 2025 In Northern Patagonia, paleontologists have unearthed an ancient lagoon ecosystem surrounded by sand dunes and palm trees where prehistoric creatures thrived. Excavations of 78 million year-old rocks, from a quarry just outside General Roca city in Argentina, yielded a treasure trove of 432 fossils belonging to over a hundred animal groups. The majority of the fossils belonged to turtles, but other residents were fish, crocodile relatives, slugs—including the first fossil record of the Neocyclotidae , a family of tropical land snails, and the first record of Leptinaria , a genus of small tropical air-breathing land snails—and dinosaurs . The most important find among them all: a new titanosaur called Chadititan calvoi. pages.description: So far, the technology has been tested only in pigs. If it's successful in humans, it could one day power tools that monitor your health or deliver drugs or electrical currents inside the body
pages.text: Scientists Invent a Digestible, Paper-Based Battery That Can Power Swallowed or Implanted Medical Devices Skip to main content Researchers tested the battery in an RFID tag that can be rolled up in a capsule and swallowed. It can then transmit information about the digestive tract to a reader outside the body. MIT News Ingestible sensors provide a helpful way to monitor a person’s health from the inside. But finding effective ways to power them has been a challenge. They typically use either standard batteries, which contain harmful chemicals, or external sources that provide energy wirelessly. Now, scientists have created digestible, paper-based batteries that can power medical devices inside the body and eventually get broken down. The technology, described in the journal Nature Chemical Engineering on September 21, has so far been tested only in pigs. If further studies confirm its safety in humans, it could one day power all sorts of medical devices. “For many of the systems we’re developing, we need power, and we power the system through different ways,” says study co-author Giovanni Traverso , a mechanical engineer at MIT and gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, in a statement . “Often, we use batteries, so the question here was: Could we develop a battery that was bioresorbable, and then apply that across a range of application areas?” Bioresorbable Batteries for Transient Ingestible Bioelectronics Watch on The battery contains electrodes made with the metals magnesium and molybdenum, which are safe for human consumption in small amounts. pages.text: Scientists may have solved the mystery of Nanotyrannus | National Geographic SCIENCE Teen T. rex or totally different dinosaur? The debate over Nanotyrannus gets a new twist. After decades of fierce debate, researchers say fossils once thought to be juvenile T. rex actually belong to a separate, sleeker species of tyrannosaur. Nanotyrannus was long thought to be the very prey it's shown attacking in the illustration above, a young Tyrannosaurus rex . New evidence suggests it was a different class of dinosaur. Anthony Hutchings By Nicholas St. Fleur Published October 30, 2025 One of paleontology’s most polarizing problems is a teenage Tyrannosaurus rex with an identity crisis, and two scientists say they’ve solved it. In 1942, researchers from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History found the skull of a small theropod in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. After scientists classified it as the new species Nanotyrannus lancensis in 1988, the skull sparked four decades of fierce debate: Do such fossils of small and slender tyrannosaurs represent a teenage version of the fearsome T. rex , or an entirely distinct dinosaur? Now, after analyzing more than 200 tyrannosaur fossils, the authors of a new study have declared that Nanotyrannus was a swift and lean dinosaur that lived alongside T. rex in the twilight of the tyrant’s reign. The conservation area is inspiring appreciation for one of the Mojave Desert's most misunderstood residents through its increasingly popular Scorpion Search Night Hikes. Led by BLM rangers, these evening programs invite participants to explore the desert after sunset and discover the fascinating world of nocturnal wildlife. Scott Milliren Scott Milliren is the Director of the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED) within the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI). In this role, he oversees a multi-billion-dollar portfolio dedicated to advancing the commercial deployment and scaling of innovative energy, materials, and industrial manufacturing technologies. His leadership supports CMEI’s mission to secure stable domestic supply chains, strengthen American manufacturing, and steward federal resources to provide affordable, reliable, and secure energy for the nation. Before joining OCED, Milliren served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, where he provided strategic guidance on organizational transformation and team development, implementing executive orders aimed at modernizing the commission. Milliren’s career spans more than three decades in the oil and gas services industry, working in both public and private sectors across all segments of energy production, including drilling, equipment manufacturing, production, and completion. pages.title: Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end - BBC Sport
pages.description: The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout in the UK have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle.
pages.text: Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Games currently cannot be shown live between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday By Dale Johnson Football issues correspondent Published 29 October 2026 The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle. The SPFL has said that it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the new deal, which will kick in from the 2029-30 season. BBC Sport understands this includes the possibility that broadcasters could bid to show all matches live - including those shown on a Saturday afternoon. The SPFL has created a tender with the greatest flexibility on the basis that the broadcaster does not seek to impose Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes. Article 48 allows leagues to set specific times when matches are banned from being shown live on television. It can only be enforced when 50% of matches in a country's top two divisions are played at the same time. While other parts of Europe have experimented with a blackout, it is now only present in the UK between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday. Other leagues now tend to stagger kick-off times so the top divisions do not all play at the same time, meaning the blackout could not be applied. In the UK, 3pm remains the traditional, default kick-off time for all leagues from the very top down through non-league. SCIENCE LAELAPS Scrappy Fossils Yield Possible Dinosaur Blood Cells By Riley Black Published June 16, 2015 • 8 min read Last week, a little movie called Jurassic World debuted. You might have heard something about it . Paleontologists certainly have been jawing about it for a while, particularly how the movie’s dinosaurs stack up against the actual animals emerging from the rock.* But all the arguments about enfluffled dinosaurs and bunny hands have missed a more fundamental issue – could scientists ever recover enough intact dinosaur goo to populate a real Jurassic World? When the first Jurassic Park premiered in 1993, finding non-avian dinosaur DNA seemed a certainty. Two days before the official release of the movie Raúl Cano and colleagues announced that they had sequenced the DNA of a 135-120 million year old, amber-encased weevil. Woodward and colleagues announced that they had sequenced DNA from an 80 million year old dinosaur bone fragment. It seemed that life had found a way. pages.title: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic
pages.description: These reptiles have roamed the oceans for 100 million years. We've put them at risk, but with a little help, they're rebounding.
pages.text: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic By Craig Welch Photographs by Thomas Peschak 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. To see all that’s hopeful and appalling about the way we treat sea turtles , there’s no better place to start than the Burj Al Arab Jumeirah hotel. This shimmering tower of blue and white glass is shaped like the jib of a sailboat bound for shore. It rose two decades ago on an artificial island amid the steel forest of construction cranes that is Dubai, part of the United Arab Emirates. A royal suite, at 8,396 square feet, comes with a private cinema and 17 pillow options. A weekend stay can top $50,000. I have come here, though, to see its nonpaying guests. ( Saving Sea Turtles) Passing a fleet of white Rolls-Royces, I meet British expat marine biologist David Robinson. We take an elevator down to a parking garage and walk by Lamborghinis to our destination: a labyrinth of pipes and plastic pools, the intensive care unit of an elaborate marine turtle hospital. In one tub a green sea turtle struggles with internal organ damage. One floor up, sick, critically endangered hawksbills fill aquariums. Blood seeps from a dying leatherback harpooned by an indigenous hunter near Indonesia’s Kei Islands. Leatherbacks are the largest of the seven sea turtle species and one of the most imperiled. The West Pacific population has fewer than a thousand females. A flatback sea turtle kicks up sand while digging a nest on Crab Island, off Australia’s northeast coast. SearchGov makes it easier for people to find the information they need from federal websites. As the search engine used by thousands of federal websites, SearchGov supports more than 200 million searches a year. SearchGov shares its history with USA.gov , beginning when internet entrepreneur Eric Brewer donated a powerful search engine to the government. In 2000, USA.gov, at the time named FirstGov.gov, debuted. It featured a search box that allowed users to search across government websites. In 2010, SearchGov expanded to serve agencies throughout the U.S. government. Learn how SearchGov helps agencies connect with the people they serve. pages.description: More than a hundred years after the USCGC Tampa sank in the deadliest U.S. naval loss of the Great War, its discovery sheds light on eleven Black sailors who made Coast Guard history.

On 26 September 1918, while operating in the English Channel, the USCGC Tampa was torpedoed and sunk by the German Submarine UB-91. All 131 persons on board were lost – the largest loss of life on any U.S. combat vessel during World War I. U.S. Coast Guard Heritage Assets Collection & Archives By Anissa Durham Published October 21, 2026 Amefike Changamire-Woodland is considered the family historian. Since the early 2000s, he has researched the life and legacy of his great-uncle Francis LeRoy Wilkes. Known to the family as “Uncle Frank,” Wilkes was a 21-year-old seaman aboard the USCGC Ta m pa during World War I. Wilkes was one of 11 Black Coast Guardsmen working on the cutter when, on Sept. 26, 1918, it was torpedoed by a German submarine. All 131 American and British men on the ship lost their lives that fateful night — the deadliest U.S. naval loss of the Great War. Some 80 years later, the fallen sailors were posthumously awarded the Purple Heart, making Wilkes and the ten other Black men onboard the first servicemen of color in the history of the Coast Guard to receive the honor. pages.description: Thousands of years ago, Florida’s coastline extended as much as 100 miles out beyond its present edge. Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America.

Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America. Archaeologists are diving the coastline that stretches from Texas to Florida to find artifacts from tribes that once lived there thousands of years ago—like these arrowheads from McFadden Beach, just outside present-day Houston. NPS The first blooms of spring. The first frost. The first dusting of snow. The signs and timing of the seasons is a finely tuned natural process. The interplay of temperature and daylight activates these changes and the subsequent plant and animal responses. A slight shift in any of these may mean that vegetation will no longer grow in a certain location or appear at a different time of year. Without plants, animals who eat them may struggle to survive or may have to move elsewhere to find better food. The consequences may extend to the entire ecosystem, including humans. In both Skagway and Nome, everyone agreed that spring is arriving earlier and fall is starting later. This not only makes for a longer growing season for gardeners, but it affects the arrival and departure timing of migratory animals that people hunt and may shift the location of where the animals are found. pages.description: Around 200 million people identifying themselves as being of African descent live in the Americas. The promotion and protection of the human rights of people of African descent  is a priority concern for the United Nations.
pages.text: Second International Decade for People of African Descent | United Nations Skip to main content UNFPA/Yuntong Man Learn & Participate: Decade for People of African Descent The Second International Decade for People of African Descent is a global effort to advance human rights, equality and opportunity for people of African descent around the world. Guided by the theme "People of African Descent: Recognition, Justice and Development," it brings together governments, the United Nations, civil society and communities to build a more just and inclusive future. Programme of Activities A Decade Dedicated to People of African Descent Recognition Justice Development Around 200 million people identifying themselves as being of African descent live in the Americas. Many millions more live in other parts of the world, outside of the African continent. The Second International Decade for People of African Descent builds on the achievements of the first Decade while accelerating action to address persistent inequalities, systemic racism, and the lasting impacts of racialised chattel enslavement and colonialism. Alyssa Schukar "The museum of the past must be set aside, reconstructed, transformed...into a nursery of living thoughts,” George Brown Goode, the first curator of the Smithsonian’s Arts and Industries Building (AIB), wrote in 1889. “It should be a house full of ideas.” AIB opened in 1881 as the first United States National Museum with a radical new philosophy. Museums could do more than research and showcase; they could teach and inspire as well. Thousands flocked to the Mall’s newest building to see firsthand the inventions that were changing the world: the electric light bulb, the steam locomotive, Alexander Graham Bell’s telephone. AIB pioneered many of the Smithsonian features we now consider essential: descriptive labels to explain what people saw, new ways of organizing displays to tell stories, and even “living animal” collections (an initiative that would eventually grow into the National Zoo). By the time I worked as a curator at the National Museum of American History , AIB was serving even younger audiences: My daughter attended preschool in the building that had once housed the Star-Spangled Banner and the Spirit of St. Louis . pages.text: See how ancient Indigenous artists left their mark on the landscape | National Geographic By Kate Nelson Photographs and video by Stephen Alvarez Published April 16, 2024 There is so much we don’t know for certain about ancient Indigenous artwork. When precisely was it made? What exactly did it mean to its creators? And yet there is still so much to be learned from these works carved into rock, painted on stone, drawn in mud, or built into the Earth’s surface. Perhaps most important is that thriving Native American societies, including my own, have inhabited Turtle Island, as many tribal peoples prefer to call North America, for tens of thousands of years. ( North America’s Native nations reassert their sovereignty: ‘We are here’. ) Considered alongside a contemporary Native reckoning—with historic Indigenous representation across everything from politics to pop culture—these sophisticated petroglyphs , pictographs, and geoglyphs help connect our past to present to future. For Native-descendant communities, this art represents a return home and a revitalization of the traditional lifeways that were all but destroyed by colonialism. On a narrow peninsula above the confluence of Rochester Wash and Muddy Creek, this sacred site is home to 13 panels of Barrier Canyon- and Fremont-style petroglyphs and pictographs. Ancient sea creatures evolved eyes with the ability to detect light more than 500 million years ago. Ever since, the sensing of light has helped animals make their way in the world. In recent times, scientists have extended our ability to sense and measure light using telescopes, microscopes, cameras, spectrometers and other devices. But just like our eyes, these classical sensors run into trouble when light becomes very faint. They need a minimum amount of light to “see” anything. And sometimes, scientists study objects so faint or distant that every photon — the fundamental unit of light — counts. In such cases, they turn to a type of quantum sensor known as a single-photon detector. These detectors come in many flavors, each with its own advantages and trade-offs. Semiconductors—materials such as silicon with tunable electrical conductivity—are the base for most electronics, enabling construction of complex integrated circuits, or chips, that power advanced technologies for healthcare, communications, computing, and transportation, among other applications. Demand for chips is already high, and that demand is growing because of uses in emerging technologies such as super intelligence, the internet of things and quantum computing. What is NIST's Role? NIST has conducted research on semiconductors since the late 1940s, when the field was created by the development of semiconductor devices called crystal diodes for radar during World War II and the invention of the transistor. NIST, then called the National Bureau of Standards (NBS), set up a lab to investigate several related topics, including semiconductors’ electrical conductivity. The NBS Semiconductor Technology Program was established in 1968 to improve measurement methods, data, reference artifacts, models and theory to enable higher device yields and reliability, lower costs, and improved fabrication and performance. Earth’s iron core generates a magnetic field that surrounds the planet and protects us from charged particles from outer space. Electric currents in wires create magnetic fields, as do the electrical signals coursing through our nerve cells. Measuring these fields can yield powerful data. Scientists measure magnetic fields produced by superconductors and other materials to design advanced technology and electronics. Biomedical researchers measure the tiny magnetic fields produced by brain cells and the electrical currents that control the heart’s beating to gather vital health information. Geologists measure magnetic minerals in rocks to study how Earth's magnetic field has evolved over the planet’s long history. And militaries around the world hope to use measurements of Earth’s magnetic field to navigate without reliance on GPS. While classical magnetometers that don’t use quantum physics, such as a compass or a flux gate magnetometer , can be good enough in some situations, quantum magnetometers are much more sensitive. By their very definition, sensors are devices that measure or detect things such as light, heat and electric current. That’s why NIST, as the nation’s measurement science institute, has been in the sensor business since its earliest years. NIST has continually developed ever-more-accurate measurement devices based on various forms of light, special materials, and quantum phenomena such as superconductivity for a broad range of applications, from aviation to medicine to communications. These sensors measure all kinds of quantities such as time, distance, mass, temperature, voltage, and fluid volume and flow. Many of the latest NIST sensors are ultra-compact and use very little power. Examples of NIST sensors include: Clocks based on the behavior of atoms in a tiny glass container on a chip. VETS Grantee Reporting System The VETS Grantee Reporting System (VGRS) is the quarterly reporting system for grant recipients of the Homeless Veterans’ Reintegration Program (HVRP) and the Jobs for Veterans States Grants (JVSG) program. Priority of Service The U.S. Department of Labor has implemented Priority of Service for veterans and eligible spouses in all qualified job training programs.
